t: Modify the Matrix — Column Maximum Replacement
o: We simply copy the matrix and overwrite every `-1` with the maximum of its column. Constraints are tiny (≤ 50×50), so any straightforward method works. In example 1, column 1 has values `{2,-1,8}` so its max is 8, replacing the `-1` at `[1][1]`; column 2 max is 9, replacing `[0][2]`. The guarantee that every column has a non-negative entry means no column is entirely `-1`.
k: Precompute each column's maximum once, then substitute.

a.n: Approach 1: Two passes over the matrix
a.i: First pass computes `colMax[j]` ignoring `-1`s (or just taking the max, since `-1` is the minimum possible value anyway). Second pass writes the answer.
s: Compute the max of each column.
Copy the matrix, replacing each `-1` with its column max.
a.t: O(m·n) — two linear scans of the grid

a.n: Approach 2: Single pass with deferred fill
a.i: Compute column maxes and fill `-1`s in one combined pass is not possible directly (max unknown yet), but you can collect `-1` coordinates during the max pass and fill afterwards, avoiding a full copy.
s: During the max pass record coordinates of every `-1`.
Afterwards write `colMax[j]` into each recorded cell.
a.sp: O(m·n) worst case for the hole list

w: Trivial warm-up problem. The only mild care point: initializing `colMax` to -1 works because -1 is the global minimum, so non-negative entries dominate automatically.
